Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The room had been open for about twenty minutes before i started, and the outside temperature was 12 degrees. We were checking the fixed extraction hood and the two flexible arms before a scheduled evening class, not doing a full building inspection. I used the checklist from the maintenance folder, but wrote the readings on a separate sheet because the printed boxes are too small for the meter numbers. The check took a little over an hour, with pauses while people moved equipment out of the way.

Malik, our technician, removed the mesh pre-filter from the fixed hood, washed it, and put it back after it had dried. He also checked the flexible arm joints and tightened the loose clamp on the arm nearest the bench grinder. I didn't remove either arm or adjust the fan controls. Malik told me the clamp had been loose for a while, but he couldn't say when it first became that way. He left the removed filter on the drying rack while we took the first readings, so the hood reading from that part of the check is not a reading with the filter installed. We put the filter back before taking the later readings.

I used the same handheld airflow meter throughout and recorded the display in metres per second. At the fixed hood, the first reading with the filter off was 5.1. With the filter back in place, the three readings were 4.6, 4.5, and 4.6. At the grinder arm, the readings after Malik tightened the clamp were 3.2, 3.3, and 3.2. At the second arm, beside the welding table, I got 2.8, 2.9, and 2.8. I wrote down the range as well as each individual number, because the display moved a little while I was holding the meter at the opening.

The readings were taken with the workshop's large roller door shut and the pedestrian door closed, although people did open the pedestrian door between sets to carry through a cart. I waited until it was shut again before starting each set. The portable fan by the paint cupboard was switched off, and the ceiling lights were on. I did not check the dust collector, the paint cupboard, or the small soldering bench, since those were outside the scope of this check. There was some grinding noise from the next room, but no one was using the grinder in our room during the measurements.

1. The fixed hood was clear of stored items, but a box of spare gloves sat on the shelf below it. The box did not cover the hood opening. I moved a stool that had been parked in front of the grinder arm, then took the measurements with the arm pulled out to the usual working position, around 35 centimetres above the bench.
2. Malik checked the date sticker on the meter and said it was due for its next service in September. I copied the serial number from the back of the meter onto my sheet, but I have not checked that number against the service log yet.
3. There was a strip of grey tape on the floor marking where the welding table usually sits. The table was about half a metre farther from the wall than the strip during the check, because a new storage cabinet had been delivered the day before. I did not move the table, and I took the arm readings in its current position.
4. The door closer on the pedestrian door worked, but the door took a few seconds to latch after it was released. I noted that because it was opened a few times during the hour, and I wanted the sheet to show the room conditions rather than suggest the door stayed closed without interruption.

Malik said, “That arm used to drift back toward the wall when you let it go.” I asked him whether it still did that after he tightened the clamp, and he said, “Not while I was standing here, but give it a proper try when the bench is in use.” I did move the arm through its normal range after the measurements; it stayed where I left it, but I didn't test it with a tool running or with material under the hood. I included Malik's comment in my notes because it describes what he observed, not because I confirmed the earlier problem myself.

The class schedule matters for how we use these results. On Friday, only the welding table is booked in the metal room, and the grinder bench is listed as clear. If both bays are used at the same time, we need to repeat the smoke check with both extraction arms positioned as they would be during work, before that setup is used for a class. The Tuesday readings were taken with neither machine running, so they do not tell us what happens when both bays are active. I have not arranged that repeat check yet, and I don't know whether the two bookings will overlap next week.

I put the meter readings, the room sketch, and Malik's note in the maintenance folder, and I kept the original paper sheet in the front pocket. The sketch marks the hood, both arm openings, the doors, and the temporary position of the welding table. Priya in building operations is the person who receives these workshop check records. Priya, could you review the sheet and let me know whether you want the mobile extraction arm moved before the next metal-room demonstration? I'm asking about the arm's position, not asking you to approve the readings as a complete inspection. If you need the smoke check repeated under the two-bay condition, please tell me who should coordinate it, since Malik is usually assigned to equipment maintenance and I handle class scheduling.

One practical detail for the next visit is that the new cabinet partly narrows the walking space beside the welding table, though it does not touch the extraction arm. The tape mark on the floor still shows the table's former position, so someone using the room sketch could mistake it for the current location unless they also read my note. I left the cabinet and table where they were, and I did not change the floor marking.
